title: Idiopathic Orbital Inflammatory Disease (IOID): The Great Mimicker
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the diagnosis and management of non-specific orbital inflammation, characterized by acute pain, proptosis, and a dramatic response to corticosteroids. Often termed 'Orbital Pseudotumor,' it remains a diagnosis of exclusion requiring rigorous workup.

sections.title: Clinical Overview & Definition
sections.content: Idiopathic Orbital Inflammatory Disease (IOID) is a benign, non-infectious, space-occupying inflammatory process of the orbit that lacks an identifiable local or systemic cause. It is characterized histologically by a polymorphous infiltrate of inflammatory cells and varying degrees of fibrosis. It is the third most common orbital disease after Thyroid Eye Disease and Lymphoproliferative disorders.

rows: Pain on eye movement, diplopia, localized redness over muscle insertion.
S-shaped upper lid deformity, tenderness in superotemporal orbit.
Uveitis, scleritis, disc edema, exudative retinal detachment.
Early vision loss (CN II), multiple CN palsies (III, IV, VI).
Disc edema, minimal vision loss initially, mimic of optic neuritis.

branches: Polymorphous Infiltrate: Lymphocytes, Plasma cells, Eosinophils

sections.title: Common Clinical Features
content: Acute onset of periorbital pain (Classic Hallmark)
Proptosis (often non-axial depending on subtype)
Eyelid erythema and edema
Chemosis and conjunctival injection
Diplopia due to painful ophthalmoplegia
Decreased visual acuity (if apical or diffuse)

sections.title: Radiological Diagnostic Signs
content: CT/MRI: Contrast enhancement of involved tissues
Myositis: Involvement of the muscle AND the tendon (Tendon-sparing = TED)
Molding: Mass often 'molds' to the shape of the globe without bone erosion
Sclerosing Variant: Low T1 and T2 signal intensity on MRI due to dense collagen
Perineuritis: 'Tram-track' enhancement around the optic nerve

sections.title: The 'Red Flags' of IOID
content: Bilateral involvement in adults (High risk of systemic disease/lymphoma)
Lack of response to systemic steroids within 48-72 hours
Evidence of bony destruction on CT (Suggests malignancy)
Numbness in V1/V2 distribution (Suggests perineural spread of tumor)
Fever and systemic malaise (Suggests infection or vasculitis)

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: Diagnostic Workup (Imaging + Labs to rule out systemic causes).
Step 2: Observation or NSAIDs for very mild, localized cases.
Step 3: Systemic Corticosteroids (Prednisone 1.0–1.5 mg/kg/day). Dramatic improvement is diagnostic support.
Step 4: Slow Steroid Taper over 6-12 weeks to prevent rebound inflammation.
Step 5: Orbital Radiation (low dose, 10-20 Gy) if steroids are contraindicated or ineffective.
Step 6: Steroid-sparing agents (Methotrexate, Mycophenolate Mofetil, or Cyclosporine).
Step 7: Biologic agents (Rituximab for IgG4-RD or Infliximab for refractory cases).

sections.title: Indications for Orbital Biopsy
content: Atypical clinical presentation
Palpable anterior orbital mass
Recurrent disease despite therapy
Failure to respond to steroids within 48-72 hours
Suspicion of lymphoma or systemic granulomatous disease

content.explanation: S: Slower onset; T: Tough fibrosis; I: IgG4-Related often; F: Fixed/Frozen globe; F: Failed steroid response (requires aggressive immunosuppression).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Pro-Tips
content: In children, IOID is more likely to be bilateral and associated with systemic symptoms (uveitis, headache).
Tolosa-Hunt Syndrome is essentially IOID extending into the cavernous sinus.
Always check serum IgG4 levels in chronic or sclerosing cases.
A 'dramatic response' to steroids is suggestive but NOT pathognomonic for IOID; some lymphomas also respond initially.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Recurrence rates vary from 30% to 50% after steroid taper.
Permanent vision loss from compressive optic neuropathy or exudative RD.
Ptosis and restrictive strabismus due to chronic fibrosis.
Phthisis bulbi in severe, untreated anterior IOID.
Prognosis is generally excellent for acute cases but guarded for sclerosing variants.
